claim: miR156 is encoded by eight coding loci (MIR156A–MIR156H) in the Arabidopsis genome.
source: In the Arabidopsis genome, miR156 is encoded by eight coding loci (MIR156A–MIR156H) (Reinhart et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reinhart et al., 2002

claim: The mir156a mir156c double mutant displayed a similar, but weak phenotype as the transgenic plant expressing a target mimicry from the constitutively active 35S promoter (35S::MIM156).
source: One of the double mutants, mir156a mir156c, displayed a similar, but weak phenotype as the transgenic plant expressing a target mimicry from the constitutively active 35S promoter (35S::MIM156), which reduced miR156 activity (Figure 1D; Franco-Zorrilla et al., 2007; Todesco et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1D showing phenotypic comparison and citations to Franco-Zorrilla et al., 2007 and Todesco et al., 2010

claim: The amount of miR156 was moderately decreased in mir156a mir156c in comparison with the wild type.

claim: The transcript levels of SPL3 and SPL9 were much higher in mir156a mir156c than in the wild type.

evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The mir156a mir156c mutant had a shortened juvenile phase compared to the wild type.
source: Compared to the wild type, the mir156a mir156c mutant had a shortened juvenile phase.
evidence: Supported by phenotypic observations described in the text

claim: The appearance of abaxial trichomes in mir156a mir156c was accelerated by 2.1 plastochrons.
source: The appearance of abaxial trichomes in mir156a mir156c was accelerated by 2.1 plastochrons (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The length-to-width ratios of the blades in mir156a mir156c were much closer to those of the adult leaves in the wild type.
source: In addition, the length-to-width ratios of the blades in mir156a mir156c were much closer to those of the adult leaves in the wild type (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by morphometric data shown in Figure 1F

claim: mir156a mir156c flowered earlier than the wild type.
source: Furthermore, mir156a mir156c flowered earlier than the wild type (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 1E

claim: MIR156A and MIR156C have dominant roles within the miR156 family in Arabidopsis.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that MIR156A and MIR156C have dominant roles within the miR156 family in Arabidopsis.
evidence: Inferred from the phenotypic and expression data presented for mir156a mir156c mutant

claim: The abundance of miR156 gradually declined over time.
source: As previously reported, the abundance of miR156 gradually declined (Figure 2A,B; Wu and Poethig, 2006; Wang et al., 2009).

claim: The transcript levels of pri-MIR156A and pri-MIR156C, but not mature miR156, exhibited damped oscillations with the highest level in the morning and lowest before dark.

claim: After transfer to constant light conditions, the oscillating expression pattern of pri-MIR156A and pri-MIR156C was no longer observed.

evidence: Supported by expression data in Figure 2D,F showing loss of oscillation under constant light

claim: The circadian clock has a negligible effect on miR156 expression.
source: After the transfer, the oscillating expression pattern of pri-MIR156A and pri-MIR156C was no longer observed (Figure 2D,F), demonstrating a negligible effect of the circadian clock on miR156 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the loss of oscillation under constant light conditions shown in Figure 2D,F

claim: The abundance of pri-MIR156A and pri-MIR156C was greatly reduced after 1 day of treatment with 50 mM sucrose, glucose, or maltose.
source: The abundance of pri-MIR156A and pri-MIR156C was greatly reduced after 1 day of treatment with 50 mM sucrose, glucose, or maltose (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3A

claim: A reduction in pri-MIR156A or pri-MIR156C was not detected when the seedlings were treated with the same concentration of mannitol or 3-O-methyl-glucose (3-OMG).
source: A reduction in pri-MIR156A or pri-MIR156C was not detected when the seedlings were treated with the same concentration of mannitol or 3-O-methyl-glucose (3-OMG), suggesting that the repression of pri-MIR156 by sugars is not due to osmotic stress.
evidence: Supported by expression data comparing sugar treatments with osmotic controls

claim: The repression of pri-MIR156 by sugars is not due to osmotic stress.
source: A reduction in pri-MIR156A or pri-MIR156C was not detected when the seedlings were treated with the same concentration of mannitol or 3-O-methyl-glucose (3-OMG), suggesting that the repression of pri-MIR156 by sugars is not due to osmotic stress.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of repression with mannitol and 3-OMG treatments

claim: Mature miR156 was decreased after 1 day of sugar treatment.
source: Consistent with the reduction in pri-MIR156 levels, mature miR156 was decreased after 1 day of sugar treatment (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The transcript levels of miR156-targeted genes, SPL9 and SPL15, were markedly increased after sugar treatment.
source: Accordingly, the transcript levels of miR156-targeted genes, SPL9 and SPL15, were markedly increased (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3B

claim: A reduction of about 40% in pri-MIR156C was observed in the seedlings treated with glucose, sucrose, or maltose for 30 min.
source: A reduction of about 40% in pri-MIR156C was observed in the seedlings treated with glucose, sucrose, or maltose, while the level of pri-MIR156C was not altered in those treated with fructose or mannitol (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The level of pri-MIR156C was not altered in seedlings treated with fructose or mannitol for 30 min.
source: A reduction of about 40% in pri-MIR156C was observed in the seedlings treated with glucose, sucrose, or maltose, while the level of pri-MIR156C was not altered in those treated with fructose or mannitol (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Glucose plays a major role in repressing miR156.
source: These results, together with the fact that glucose is the common hydrolytic product shared by sucrose and maltose, suggest that glucose plays a major role in repressing miR156.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that glucose is the common product of sucrose and maltose, both of which repress miR156

claim: The expression of pri-MIR156 transcripts except pri-MIR156B was reduced after glucose treatment.
source: The expression of other pri-MIR156 transcripts except pri-MIR156B was reduced after glucose treatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Sugar-depleted seedlings exhibited a higher expression level of miR156 compared to seedlings grown in media supplemented with sugar under normal light conditions.
source: Compared to the seedlings grown in 1/2 MS liquid media supplemented with sugar under normal light conditions, the sugar-depleted seedlings exhibited a higher expression level of miR156 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by expression data from sugar starvation experiment shown in Figure 3E

claim: The levels of pri-MIR159A, pri-MIR159B, and pri-MIR165A were not reduced after sugar treatment.
source: The levels of all these transcripts were not reduced after sugar treatment (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Sugar specifically represses miR156.
source: To investigate whether sugar specifically represses miR156, we analyzed the expression of other miRNA primary transcripts, including pri-MIR159A, pri-MIR159B, and pri-MIR165A. The levels of all these transcripts were not reduced after sugar treatment (Figure 3F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that other miRNA primary transcripts are not repressed by sugar

claim: miR156 was highly abundant in 15-day-old plants but less so in 60-day-old plants grown under short day conditions.
source: Expression analyses demonstrated that miR156 was highly abundant in 15-day-old plants but less so in 60-day-old plants (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 4A

claim: 60-day-old plants exhibited a higher level of glucose, fructose, and sucrose than 15-day-old plants.
source: In contrast to this expression pattern, 60-day-old plants exhibited a higher level of glucose, fructose, and sucrose than 15-day-old plants (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by sugar measurement data shown in Figure 4B

claim: There is an inverse correlation between the level of miR156 and endogenous sugar content in vivo.
source: These results are consistent with our findings that sugar represses miR156 and indicate an inverse correlation between the level of miR156 and endogenous sugar content in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that miR156 is high when sugar is low and vice versa

claim: The removal of the first two leaves resulted in an increased level of miR156 in the shoot apices.
source: Consistent with the previous report (Yang et al. 2011), the removal of the first two leaves resulted in an increased level of miR156 in the shoot apices (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 4F and citation to Yang et al. 2011

claim: The production of abaxial trichomes in the defoliated plants was delayed by 1.0 plastochrons compared to intact plants.
source: Compared to intact plants, the production of abaxial trichomes in the defoliated plants was delayed by 1.0 plastochrons (Figure 4D), and the increase in the length-to-width ratio of the lamina was slower (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The increase in the length-to-width ratio of the lamina was slower in defoliated plants.
source: Compared to intact plants, the production of abaxial trichomes in the defoliated plants was delayed by 1.0 plastochrons (Figure 4D), and the increase in the length-to-width ratio of the lamina was slower (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by morphometric data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Sucrose application partially suppressed the delay in the juvenile-to-adult phase transition caused by defoliation.
source: Sucrose application partially suppressed the delay in the juvenile-to-adult phase transition caused by defoliation.
evidence: Supported by phenotypic observations described in the text

claim: The sucrose-treated plants produced the abaxial trichomes 0.8 plastochrons later than intact wild type plants, but 1.6 plastochrons earlier than the mannitol-treated plants.
source: The sucrose-treated plants produced the abaxial trichomes 0.8 plastochrons later than intact wild type plants, but 1.6 plastochrons earlier than the mannitol-treated plants (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phenotypic data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The length-to-width ratios of the fifth, seventh, and ninth leaves in the sucrose-treated plants were higher than those in the mannitol-treated plants.
source: In addition, the length-to-width ratios of the fifth, seventh, and ninth leaves in the sucrose-treated plants were higher than those in the mannitol-treated plants (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by morphometric data shown in Figure 4E

claim: The expression of miR156 was reduced in the apices of the sucrose-treated plants but not in those treated with mannitol.
source: In agreement with these phenotypic differences, the expression of miR156 was reduced in the apices of the sucrose-treated plants but not in those treated with mannitol (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 4F

claim: A mutation in CAO/CH1 (At1g44446), which encodes chlorophyll (Chl) a oxygenase, causes a reduced level of Chl b and low efficiency of photosynthesis.
source: A mutation in CAO/CH1 (At1g44446), which encodes chlorophyll (Chl) a oxygenase, causes a reduced level of Chl b and low efficiency of photosynthesis (Espineda et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Espineda et al., 1999

claim: The cao/ch1 mutant developed smaller pale green leaves and had a prolonged juvenile phase compared to the wild type.
source: Compared to the wild type, the cao/ch1 mutant developed smaller pale green leaves and had a prolonged juvenile phase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The rosette leaves in the cao/ch1 mutant were rounder than those in the wild type plant.
source: The rosette leaves in the cao/ch1 mutant were rounder than those in the wild type plant (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by morphometric data shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: The appearance of abaxial trichomes in the cao/ch1 mutant was delayed.
source: Additionally, the appearance of abaxial trichomes in the cao/ch1 mutant was delayed (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Higher levels of miR156 accumulated in the cao/ch1 mutant than in the wild type plant.
source: Expression analyses indicated that higher levels of miR156 accumulated in the cao/ch1 mutant than in the wild type plant (Figure 5D).

claim: 35S::MIM156 cao/ch1 produced the abaxial trichomes on the first leaf, and the leaves were elongated and serrated.
source: Similarly to 35S::MIM156, 35S::MIM156 cao/ch1 produced the abaxial trichomes on the first leaf, and the leaves were elongated and serrated (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The cao/ch1 mutants exhibited higher glucose sensitivity compared to the wild type.
source: Compared to the wild type, the cao/ch1 mutants exhibited higher glucose sensitivity.
evidence: Supported by expression data described in the text

claim: Treatment of cao/ch1 seedlings with 50 mM glucose significantly reduced the level of miR156.
source: Treatment of cao/ch1 seedlings with 50 mM glucose significantly reduced the level of miR156 (Figure 5E).

claim: Sugar from the pre-existing leaves acts as a mobile signal to trigger the juvenile-to-adult phase transition through repression of miR156 in the young leaf primordia.
source: Taken together, we conclude that sugar from the pre-existing leaves acts as a mobile signal to trigger the juvenile-to-adult phase transition through repression of miR156 in the young leaf primordia.

claim: miR156 is present in all major plant taxa.
source: miR156 is present in all major plant taxa (Axtell and Bowman, 2008).

claim: The amount of miR156 was greatly reduced in all the sucrose-treated plants (N. benthamiana, S. lycopersicum, and P. patens) compared to those treated with mannitol.
source: Compared to those treated with mannitol, the amount of miR156 was greatly reduced in all the sucrose-treated plants (Figure 6), indicating that repression of miR156 by sugar is evolutionarily conserved.

claim: Repression of miR156 by sugar is evolutionarily conserved.
source: Compared to those treated with mannitol, the amount of miR156 was greatly reduced in all the sucrose-treated plants (Figure 6), indicating that repression of miR156 by sugar is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that sugar represses miR156 in multiple plant species

claim: The promoter fragments (harboring TATA boxes) of MIR156A and MIR156C were substantially enriched in the mannitol-treated seedlings, but not in those treated with glucose.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, the promoter fragments (harboring TATA boxes) of MIR156A and MIR156C were substantially enriched in the mannitol-treated seedlings, but not in those treated with glucose, indicating that glucose induces transcriptional repression of MIR156A and MIR156C (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Glucose induces transcriptional repression of MIR156A and MIR156C.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, the promoter fragments (harboring TATA boxes) of MIR156A and MIR156C were substantially enriched in the mannitol-treated seedlings, but not in those treated with glucose, indicating that glucose induces transcriptional repression of MIR156A and MIR156C (Figure 7A).
evidence: Inferred from ChIP data showing reduced RNA Pol II binding at MIR156A/C promoters after glucose treatment

claim: The transcript level of HXK1 was increased about fourfold after 3 h of glucose treatment.
source: The transcript level of HXK1 was increased about fourfold after 3 h of glucose treatment.
evidence: Supported by expression data described in the text

claim: The expression of HXK1 was not altered in the seedlings treated with glucose and ActD.
source: By contrast, the expression of HXK1 was not altered in the seedlings treated with glucose and ActD (Figure 7B).

claim: The addition of ActD did not affect repression of pri-MIR156C by glucose.

evidence: Supported by expression data described in the text

claim: The transcript level of pri-MIR156C was reduced by about 75% after 3 hr in the presence of glucose, compared to a 30% reduction in the presence of mannitol.

claim: Glucose regulates the abundance of pri-MIR156 independently of the miRNA processing machinery.
source: Similar to the wild type, the amount of pri-MIR156A and pri-MIR156C was markedly decreased in the ActD/glucose-treated se-3 mutant (Figure 7C,D), indicating that glucose regulates the abundance of pri-MIR156 independently of the miRNA processing machinery.

claim: gin2-1 exhibited a lower level of miR156 than the wild type.

claim: The expression of miR156 still decreased over time in the gin2-1 mutant.

claim: An evident decrease in pri-MIR156C was observed in the gin2-1 seedlings treated with ActD/glucose.

claim: HXK1 plays a role in miR156 expression but is not absolutely required for the repression of miR156 by sugar.

claim: The level of pri-MIR156C transcripts was greatly reduced in the ActD-treated samples, but not in those treated with both ActD and CHX.

claim: Sugar-induced pri-MIR156C degradation requires de novo protein synthesis.

claim: The expression of pri-MIR156A and pri-MIR156C was slightly increased in upf1-5 and upf3-1 mutants compared to the wild type.

claim: Sugar promotes pri-MIR156 degradation independently of canonical NMD.
